name: Cannabis use disorder
summary: No medication is FDA-approved for cannabis use disorder or cannabis withdrawal. Psychosocial treatments (CBT, motivational enhancement, contingency management) are first-line. Pharmacotherapy evidence is limited and mixed (Cochrane 2019). Investigational agents such as AEF0117 and PP-01 remain in clinical trials.
plainSummary: Cannabis use disorder means having trouble cutting back on marijuana even when it causes problems. No medicine is approved for it, so counseling is the main treatment; a few medicines are being studied.
noApprovedNote: No FDA-approved medication exists for cannabis use disorder or cannabis withdrawal as of October 2026. Searches for 2024–2026 FDA approvals found none; candidates such as AEF0117 and PP-01 are still investigational. All options below are off-label with limited evidence.

offLabel.use: Reduce cannabis use and withdrawal symptoms (sleep, craving)
offLabel.notes: A small 12-week proof-of-concept RCT (1200 mg/day) found reduced use and withdrawal symptoms, but it has not been replicated in large trials. Cautions: sedation, misuse potential (especially with opioids), and renal dosing.

references.label: Mason BJ, et al. A proof-of-concept randomized controlled study of gabapentin in cannabis dependence. Neuropsychopharmacology 2012
Nielsen S, et al. Pharmacotherapies for cannabis dependence. Cochrane 2019

offLabel.use: Adjunct to contingency management, mainly studied in adolescents
offLabel.notes: A 2012 adolescent RCT (1200 mg twice daily) doubled the odds of negative urine tests, but a large adult trial and a 2025 youth trial did not confirm benefit. Generally well tolerated (GI upset).

references.label: Gray KM, et al. N-acetylcysteine in cannabis-dependent adolescents. Am J Psychiatry 2012
N-acetylcysteine for youth cannabis use disorder: randomized controlled trial main findings. Neuropsychopharmacology 2025

offLabel.notes: A 2019 Cochrane review found that THC preparations (including nabiximols, not available in the US) may reduce withdrawal and improve retention but do not clearly increase abstinence. Cautions: dronabinol is C-III and nabilone C-II; sedation, psychoactive effects, and misuse potential.

references.label: Nielsen S, et al. Pharmacotherapies for cannabis dependence. Cochrane 2019

offLabel.notes: A 2026 phase 2 RCT (n=174) found no effect overall, with reduced use in men but not women. Evidence is insufficient to support routine use. Cautions: nausea and abnormal dreams. May be reasonable to consider when tobacco is co-used.

references.label: McRae-Clark AL, et al. Varenicline for cannabis use disorder: a randomized controlled trial. Addiction 2026
